text.en: Raju saw a model of an atom with a tiny centre and circling dots. "Is the atom like a small solar system?" he asked.

In experiments led by Ernest Rutherford, researchers observed how some alpha particles changed direction near gold atoms. The observations supported a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. Bohr’s historical model assigned electrons to specific energy levels around the nucleus. The innermost shell, called K, is the lowest in energy in the shell model used here.
The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number Z and the sum of protons and neutrons is its mass number A. Electrons are arranged in shells as the electronic configuration, such as 2, 8, 3 for aluminium. The outermost shell is the valence shell, and the combining capacity of an element is its valency.
Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are isotopes, atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are isobars, and atoms with the same number of neutrons are isotones. The chapter also gives the laws of chemical combination such as the law of multiple proportions.

The chapter also gives the laws of chemical combination such as the law of multiple proportions.
Begin with three particles: a proton has a positive charge, an electron has a negative charge, and a neutron has no net electric charge.
Protons and neutrons belong to the nucleus. Electrons account for most of the size of the atom through the region they occupy, while the nucleus accounts for nearly all the mass.

board.text: Tiny nucleus contains nearly all the mass

text.en: Before the nuclear model, Thomson described negative electrons in a spread-out region of positive charge. Rutherford’s experimental evidence supported a different arrangement of that positive charge.

On a diagram of the historical scattering results, most marked paths carry straight on and a few turn sharply. Explain how a very small region of concentrated charge can account for both observations.

board.text: Most paths nearly straight · a few turn sharply

text.en: The classical orbit picture could not account for stable atoms or their observed spectra. Bohr allowed certain energies, which helped explain the spectrum of hydrogen.
A ring diagram is a way to organise electron counts. In modern models, an orbital describes where an electron is likely to be found, without giving it a track like a planet’s orbit.

board.text: Orbital describes a region of probability

text.en: The simple Bohr picture works best for hydrogen and similar one-electron systems. More detailed models account for atoms with several electrons. Quantum numbers label features of the states available to electrons.
Chadwick’s work provided evidence for the neutron. It carries no charge and has a mass close to a proton’s, which helps explain how nuclei can differ in mass without differing in charge.

board.text: Neutron adds mass without electric charge

text.en: An atomic number of thirteen identifies aluminium because it has thirteen protons. If the atom is neutral, it also has thirteen electrons. The proton count identifies the element even if its electron count changes in an ion.
Take a mass number of twenty-seven for this aluminium nucleus. Subtract the thirteen protons to find the neutron count, which is fourteen.
Read standard nuclide notation by looking at the upper and lower numbers on the left of the symbol. The upper number is mass number and the lower number is atomic number.
Mass number is the whole-number count of nucleons in one nucleus. An element’s listed average atomic mass can reflect its different isotopes, and its numerical value need not be a whole number.

board.text: A counts protons and neutrons in one nucleus

text.en: The shell diagram for neutral aluminium puts two electrons in K and eight in L. Three remain in the next occupied shell, so the configuration is two, eight, three.

A shell labelled by number n can hold at most two times n squared electrons. That gives capacity eighteen for the third shell, although some next electrons occupy a lower-energy option in the fourth shell before the third is full.
For neutral calcium in the first twenty elements, read the simplified shell counts as two, eight, eight and two. The last two are valence electrons because they occupy the outermost shell.
Valency describes combining capacity in simple compounds. Chlorine has seven valence electrons and often gains or shares one in a simple bond, so its common valency in those examples is one.
Compare carbon twelve and carbon thirteen. Both nuclei have six protons, while the first has six neutrons and the second has seven. Their matching atomic number makes them isotopes of carbon.
Argon forty and calcium forty have matching mass numbers but different proton counts. They are called isobars. The different proton counts also mean they are different elements.
Carbon fourteen and nitrogen fifteen both have eight neutrons. Confirm by subtracting each element’s atomic number from its mass number. Equal neutron counts make them isotones.

Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide contain different masses of oxygen for a fixed carbon mass. The oxygen masses are sixteen and thirty-two for twelve mass units of carbon, making the small whole-number ratio one to two.

One carbon atom bonds to four hydrogen atoms in methane and two oxygen atoms in carbon dioxide. The corresponding hydrogen and oxygen masses are four and thirty-two. Their ratio of one to eight also occurs in water.

The combining-volumes law compares gas volumes under the same temperature and pressure. A balanced equation can show simple whole-number ratios for gases. Read the coefficients as volume ratios only under the matching conditions.

board.text: Gas-volume comparison: same temperature and pressure

text.en: Test yourself with any isotope symbol. Read its proton count, subtract to find the neutrons, and state whether the atom is neutral before deciding how many electrons to draw.

board.text: Identify Z → compute A − Z → check charge

problem.en: An aluminium-27 atom is neutral. Its atomic number is 13. Find its particle counts and shell configuration.

text.en: Use atomic number thirteen for the number of protons, and subtract thirteen from mass number twenty-seven.

why.en: The nucleus contains thirteen protons and fourteen neutrons.

text.en: Use thirteen electrons because the atom is neutral.

why.en: The negative electron charge balances the positive proton charge.

text.en: Place two electrons in K and eight in L, leaving three in M.

why.en: The shell configuration is two, eight, three.

prompt.en: A friend says The atom is mostly the nucleus. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Rutherford found the nucleus is tiny.
Most of the atom is empty space where electrons move.

points.en: Shell configurations describe how electrons are grouped by energy level.
Isotopes share the atomic number but not the mass number.
